fvg-main.title: I Tested Every Fair Value Gap for a Year (Gold & Nasdaq)
fvg-main.desc:
Price comes back to fill the gap, and the gap acts like a floor. Everyone draws it. I counted what price actually did after every fair value gap for a year, on gold and Nasdaq futures, and traded one written rule after costs.

Price came back to the gap about 8 times in 10. Once it came back, the gap held only about 3 times in 10.
Win rate about one in three on a 2:1 target. After costs the average trade gave back about a tenth of the risk. Worst losing run: 13 on gold, 25 on Nasdaq.
Larger gaps held more often (about 4 in 10 vs 1 in 5 for the smallest), found after looking, so an idea to test forward, not a finding.

pfs-short-B.title: Your prop firm loss limit moves. Do you know how? #propfirm #shorts
pfs-short-B.desc:
The biggest difference between rule books is the floor: your maximum loss.

Static: poured in concrete, it never moves.
End-of-day trailing: comes up behind you only after a higher close.
Trailing during the day: follows your best open profit. A trade that was up $500 and closed flat has still lifted your floor by $500.

gs-main.title: Gold Sweeps Yesterday's Low. Does It Snap Back?
gs-main.desc:
Gold takes out yesterday's low and snaps right back. Everyone calls it a sweep, and everyone wants to buy it. So I counted every one of them for a year.

Gold took out yesterday's low on about half of all days: 124 times in a year. It closed back above the low on about 47% of them. Close to a coin flip.
Depth decided more than the sweep itself: once gold was already $20 below the low, about 1 in 4 came back by the close. $50 below, about 1 in 10.
The next day: after a breakdown day, the next day took out that low about 6 times in 10, and still closed higher a bit under 6 times in 10.
Nasdaq futures, same rule: almost the same answer.

pbe-main.title: How Many Payouts to Break Even?
pbe-main.desc:
Your first payout feels like profit. Before you celebrate, ask one question: how many payouts does it take just to pay back what it cost to get here?

In one worked example (attempt $150, activation $100, pass 1 in 3, first payout 1 in 2), every first payout needs about six attempts and two passes: $1,100 in fees. A $1,000 payout at a 90% split puts $900 in your hand, so you are still $200 behind.
Moving the split from 80% to 90% changed that by $100. Moving the pass rate from 1 in 3 to 1 in 2 changed it three times as far.
And over a simulated year, traders with exactly the same skill ended anywhere from about $1,900 down to $3,250 up, only because of the order the luck came in.

nfb-main.title: Nasdaq Breaks Yesterday's High. How Often Is It Fake?
nfb-main.desc:
Nasdaq breaks yesterday's high, everyone buys the breakout, and then it falls straight back through. So I counted every break of yesterday's high for a whole year.

Nasdaq took out yesterday's high on a little over half of all days: 136 times. About 6 in 10 held to the close. About 4 in 10 were fake.
Distance was the tell: once price was about 100 points above the high, about 3 in 4 held. Past about 200 points, more than 9 in 10. Breaks that never got 100 points of room failed about 8 times in 10.
The retest was the normal path: of breakouts that ran at least 50 points, about 9 in 10 came back to the level later that day, and those still held about 2 times in 3.
Gold futures, same rule: more fakes, but the same distance story.

td-main.title: The Drawdown Line That Follows You (Trailing Drawdown, Explained)
td-main.desc:
Your balance is up on the day, and yet the room you have left is smaller than this morning. That is how a trailing drawdown works: a line that follows you up and never follows you back down.

Three kinds of line: static, end of day, and intraday. On one real Nasdaq day (23 June 2026, one micro), the same trade and the same close left about $1,864 of room under a static or end-of-day line, and about $1,206 under an intraday line. About 40% of the room, gone on a small red day.
About 65% of red Nasdaq days and 61% of red gold days were at least $100 green first.
Then the lock, and an example trader over 60 days: how often each kind of line got touched, with and without the lock.
